The town hired a man to listen to the bridge.

It was an old bridge, older than anyone’s grandmother, built from gray stone and a kind of confidence no longer available locally. It crossed a river that was usually shallow enough to embarrass a bridge, except in March, when the water rose and everyone remembered why their ancestors had bothered.

The man’s name was Ellis. He had no particular qualifications, but neither had the other applicants.

“What would you listen for?” the council asked.

“Changes,” he said.

This impressed them because it was both sensible and inexpensive.

They gave him a folding chair, a notebook, and a small brass badge that said MUNICIPAL LISTENER. Each morning he sat beneath the central arch. He listened to the river, the tires overhead, the tiny settling noises of stone. At noon he ate a cheese sandwich. At four he went home.

For the first three months, his reports were brief.

*Monday: Nothing unusual.*

*Tuesday: Nothing unusual.*

*Wednesday: A shopping cart passed downstream. Otherwise normal.*

The council was pleased. Here, finally, was a public service producing reassuring results.

Then, one Thursday, Ellis heard someone say his name.

Not loudly. Not mysteriously, either. It sounded like a person in another room who needed a jar opened.

“Ellis.”

He got up and walked around the arch.

Nobody.

He sat down.

“Ellis.”

He looked at the bridge.

“Yes?”

A truck passed overhead. Dust drifted from a seam in the stone.

“Your sandwich,” said the bridge. “There’s an ant.”

Ellis inspected his lunch. There was indeed an ant, negotiating the crust.

“Thank you.”

“Of course.”

He moved the ant to the grass.

That afternoon, his report read:

*Thursday: Minor insect activity.*

He did not consider this dishonest. The form had no section for conversations.

***

The bridge turned out to be interested in ordinary things.

It asked whether people still danced at weddings. It wanted to know what had happened to the horses. Ellis explained engines, badly, and the bridge listened with the politeness of someone who had already grasped the essentials.

“Explosions,” it said.

“Small ones.”

“And you sit beside them?”

“More or less.”

The bridge considered this.

“The horses must be relieved.”

Sometimes it asked about people Ellis did not know.

A woman with yellow gloves. A boy who had dropped a silver cup into the river. Two brothers who used to cross together and then, for many years, separately.

“I don’t remember their names,” the bridge said.

“Did you ever know them?”

“No.”

“Then you haven’t forgotten.”

The bridge was quiet for the rest of the morning.

Later it said, “That is a useful distinction.”

***

Ellis had been married once. His wife, Mara, had died four years before he became a municipal listener.

He did not tell the bridge immediately. It learned by asking why he always made two sandwiches and brought only one.

“I put the other in the refrigerator,” he said.

“For tomorrow?”

“Usually.”

“Does it keep?”

“Not especially.”

The river moved around a branch caught between two rocks.

After a while, Ellis said, “I know I could just make one.”

“I didn’t ask that,” said the bridge.

He liked it better after that.

***

In November, an engineer arrived wearing clean boots and carrying instruments in padded cases.

Ellis watched her attach sensors to the stone.

“Any unusual sounds?” she asked.

“Define unusual.”

“Cracking. Grinding. Sharp reports under load.”

“No sharp reports.”

She glanced at his notebook.

“What exactly do you write down?”

“Changes.”

She nodded, much as the council had.

For two days she measured, tapped, frowned, and entered numbers into a tablet. On the third day she sat beside Ellis beneath the arch.

“It needs work,” she said.

“How much?”

“A lot.”

“Will they do it?”

She looked up at the underside of the roadway.

“They might replace it.”

That evening, Ellis stayed after four.

“You heard?” he asked.

“Yes.”

“Are you frightened?”

“I don’t know,” said the bridge. “What does frightened feel like?”

Ellis thought.

“Like trying to prepare for something by imagining it repeatedly.”

Water ticked against the stones.

“Then yes.”

***

The council held a public meeting.

People loved the bridge, provided loving it did not significantly affect taxes or traffic. They called it irreplaceable, then asked what a replacement would cost.

Ellis stood at the back with his badge pinned to his coat.

When public comments opened, he approached the microphone.

He had prepared a speech about memory. He had written phrases like *shared inheritance* and *the fabric of this community*. Reading it over, he had been embarrassed to find he sounded exactly like a man asking for money.

So he folded the paper.

“I spend every day under that bridge,” he said. “The engineer says it can be repaired.”

Someone asked how he could justify the expense.

“I can’t,” Ellis said. “I wouldn’t know how. But I’d like us to get an estimate before we decide.”

The council agreed to get an estimate.

It was a smaller victory than he had hoped for on his walk to the meeting, and a larger one than he had expected while waiting to speak.

***

The work began in April.

Ellis’s chair had to be moved beyond the safety barriers. He disliked the new spot; the bank sloped, and one of the chair’s feet sank into mud. Between machinery and running water, he could hear nothing from the arch.

He still came each morning.

One day the engineer brought him a flat piece of timber to put beneath the chair.

“Better?” she asked.

He tested it.

“Much.”

When she left, he opened his notebook. He recorded the delivery of stone, the weather, and a loose bolt he had noticed in the temporary fence.

Then he unwrapped his sandwich.

From somewhere beneath the scaffolding came a voice, faint but distinct.

“What have you got today?”

“Cheese.”

“Again?”

“It’s what I like.”

“Fair enough,” said the bridge.
